Renal control of pH.a: Draw two tubule cells side by side. In the first, a proximal tubule cell reclaiming filtered bicarbonate: hydrogen ion secreted into the lumen, carbonic anhydrase there, carbon dioxide crossing into the cell, bicarbonate returned to blood. In the second, an intercalated cell generating new bicarbonate by pumping hydrogen ion onto phosphate or ammonia buffer. One line: say which of the two can push plasma bicarbonate above where it started, and why the other one cannot.
Renal control of pH.b: Draw one set of axes, time in hours to days on the x and arterial pH on the y with the band 7.35 to 7.45 marked. Load the patient with metabolic acid at time zero, then plot two correction curves, the respiratory response and the renal response, each starting when it really starts and reaching as far as it really gets. One line: say why the fast one cannot finish the job, and name what the slow one is physically excreting.

The four acid base disorders.a: Draw a two by two grid, respiratory and metabolic down the side, acidosis and alkalosis across the top. Write the normal values once at the top: pH 7.35 to 7.45, PCO2 35 to 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 to 26 mEq/L. In every cell draw three arrows for pH, PCO2, and bicarbonate pointing the right way, and circle the one that is the primary disturbance. One line: state the single rule that identifies the primary value, using the direction of pH.
The four acid base disorders.b: Draw four patients, one per disorder, each with the organ or process that caused it and the blood gas numbers it would produce. Do not use diabetic ketoacidosis, pick your own metabolic acidosis. Mark the primary change on the drawing itself so it is visible without reading. One line: two of your four have a low pH, so name the single value that separates them and say which way it points in each.

Compensation.a: Draw one time axis for a patient in respiratory acidosis with three vertical slices on it, uncompensated, partially compensated, and fully compensated. At each slice draw pH, PCO2, and bicarbonate as small bars against their normal bands. Show bicarbonate climbing while PCO2 stays high, and pH walking back into range. One line: at the fully compensated slice two values are still abnormal, so say which one still tells you what the original problem was.
Compensation.b: Draw two blood gas sets that both read pH 7.32, one a respiratory acidosis partly compensated by the kidney and one a metabolic acidosis partly compensated by the lung. Draw the compensating organ in each with the actual action it is taking, retaining bicarbonate or blowing off carbon dioxide. Mark on each which value is the disturbance and which is the response. One line: say why compensation never carries pH past 7.4 to the other side.

Arterial blood gas interpretation.a: Draw a decision tree you could use cold, with a blood gas at the top. Branch first on pH, low, high, or in range. Branch next on which of PCO2 and bicarbonate moved the way that would cause that pH. Branch last on whether the other moved to oppose it. End every path in a named disorder and its compensation state, then run one set of numbers down your tree. One line: say what a pH of exactly 7.40 with both other values abnormal means.
Arterial blood gas interpretation.b: Draw three patients with a short clinical picture each: a severe asthma attack, two days of vomiting, and shock with poor tissue perfusion. Beside each draw pH, PCO2, and bicarbonate as arrows against their normal bands, and mark which value is the primary disturbance. One line: pick the one where you would treat the underlying cause rather than the number, and say what would go wrong if you chased the number instead.

Multisystem integration case.a: Pick a disturbance from this term, not dehydration, and draw it crossing at least three organ systems. Set the page up as a chain of organs rather than a list: the insult, the first system to respond, what it changes, and the next system reacting to that change. Number every arrow in the order things actually happen and mark where a slow step lags. One line: name the point where a compensation creates a second problem, and say what that second problem is.
Multisystem integration case.b: Draw a person who has lost about a liter of blood, then draw the response across four panels on one page, seconds, minutes, hours, and days. Seconds gets the baroreceptor reflex. Minutes gets fluid shifting from interstitium into the capillaries. Hours gets renin angiotensin aldosterone and ADH acting on the kidney. Days gets erythropoietin and the marrow. One line: say which panel restores blood pressure and which restores oxygen carrying, and why those are not the same problem.

Exercise as an integrated response.a: Draw one time axis from rest through twenty minutes of moderate exercise and stack five curves on it: heart rate, cardiac output, ventilation, muscle blood flow, and renal blood flow. Get the directions and the relative sizes right, including the one that falls. Mark where each begins to move. One line: total peripheral resistance drops while mean arterial pressure rises, so say how both of those can be true at the same time.
Exercise as an integrated response.b: Draw a working muscle in the middle of the page with five systems running into it as spokes: cardiovascular delivering oxygen, respiratory loading it, endocrine supplying fuel with the hormones named, renal conserving salt and water, and the muscle itself putting out heat and carbon dioxide. On every spoke draw the actual molecule moving and its direction. One line: pick the system that sets the limit on how long you can hold this intensity, and say what runs out.

Drawing based synthesis check.a: Pick any homeostatic loop from this term that you have not already drawn twice, close everything, and draw it complete from memory: stimulus, receptor, afferent path, integrating center, efferent path, effector, response, and the arrow closing back onto the stimulus. Name the real anatomical structure at every position rather than a generic box. One line: mark the single step you were least certain about while drawing, and say what you would check to settle it.
Drawing based synthesis check.b: Pick one regulated variable, your choice, and draw it pushed off its set point and then corrected twice on the same time axis, once by a fast neural reflex and once by a slow hormonal loop. Show the two responses starting at different times and correcting by different amounts. Label the receptor, center, and effector for each. One line: say what the fast loop buys you given that the slow one was going to fix it anyway.
